title: Are stupid people happier?
summary: Josh and Chuck explore whether less intelligent people are happier, starting with quotes from Hemingway, Charles de Gaulle, and others. They cite a study of about 14,000 people (reported on the Freakonomics blog) finding the top third in vocabulary and analytical reasoning tests reported being happiest, and discuss the problems with studying happiness: it is subjective, self-reported, and studied by smart people. They touch on gifted kids being separated in school, then discuss positive psychology (Martin Seligman, University of Pennsylvania), the ethics of happiness pills, and acceptance and commitment therapy, with Josh sharing a childhood firecracker story. The episode closes with a listener email about how TV shows like CSI distort real forensic work, and a T-shirt giveaway offer to that listener.

segments.title: Opening banter and quotes on happiness and dumbness
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open with banter and a sponsor tag, then Josh asks whether Chuck is happy and jokingly calls him dumb. They trade quotes from Hemingway, Charles de Gaulle, and Charlton Heston.

segments.title: Defining intelligence and the link to happiness
segments.summary: The hosts discuss whether the question concerns emotional, intellectual, or street intelligence, and how IQ scores relate to happiness. They reference a study of about 14,000 people in which the top third on vocabulary and analytical reasoning tests reported being happiest.

segments.title: Problems with studying happiness
segments.summary: Josh argues that happiness is subjective and that the field is studied by intelligent people who think about happiness, so it undermines itself. Gifted children being separated in school is raised briefly. Studies rely on self-reported surveys, which are generally discarded in other sciences.

segments.title: Positive psychology and ethics of happiness pills
segments.summary: The hosts discuss positive psychology, a subfield associated with Martin Seligman at the University of Pennsylvania, and its focus on interventions moving people from zero to positive eight. They raise ethical questions about a pill that could make normal people happy.

segments.title: Acceptance and commitment therapy
segments.summary: Josh introduces acceptance and commitment therapy as a contrary approach that acknowledges negative experiences rather than suppressing them. He tells a childhood story about stealing firecrackers and how it still affects him. Chuck says his own approach is closer to this view, and they discuss people who simply bliss out.

segments.title: Wrap-up of the happiness question
segments.summary: The hosts conclude that whether stupid people are happier is unknown and depends on which self-reported survey one reads. They invite listeners to comment on the blog.

segments.title: Listener email on CSI and forensic TV
segments.summary: A listener describes his wife's carjacking and assault, and how the attacker's cigarette with DNA led to an arrest through CODIS. He says TV like CSI misrepresented the process, and that FBI and forensic staff at a CODIS conference criticized the CSI effect. The hosts joke about T-shirts and invite listeners to send their own stories.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Closing sponsor tag and sign-off for the episode.
